title: Python Fundamentals
description: Core Python syntax and built-in behavior for people learning the language

questions.question: Which built-in function returns the number of items in a list?
questions.explanation: len() is the built-in that returns the number of items in a sequence or collection, such as len([1, 2, 3]) returning 3. count() is a list method that counts occurrences of a specific value.

questions.question: What is the result of 7 // 2 in Python 3?
questions.explanation: The // operator is floor division: it divides and rounds down to the nearest whole number, so 7 // 2 is 3. Regular division with / would give 3.5.

questions.question: Which of these built-in types is mutable (can be changed after creation)?
questions.explanation: Lists are mutable, so you can append, remove, or reassign elements in place. Tuples, strings, and integers are immutable, and any operation that appears to modify them actually creates a new object.

questions.question: Which character begins a single-line comment in Python?
questions.explanation: Python uses # to start a comment, and everything after it on that line is ignored by the interpreter. The other symbols are comment markers in languages such as C, Java, and SQL.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to define a named function in Python?
questions.explanation: A named function is created with the def keyword, as in def greet(name):. The other spellings come from other languages and are not valid Python keywords.

questions.question: In Python 3, what type does the input() function return?
questions.explanation: input() always returns a string, even when the user types digits. You must convert it explicitly, for example with int(input()), before doing arithmetic on it.

questions.question: What is the index of the first element in a Python list?
questions.explanation: Python uses zero-based indexing, so the first element is at index 0. The index -1 is a valid shortcut for the last element.

questions.question: Which statement is used to handle runtime errors in Python?
questions.explanation: Python catches exceptions with a try block followed by one or more except blocks. try/catch is Java and JavaScript syntax, and begin/rescue is Ruby.

questions.question: Given nums = [10, 20, 30, 40], what does nums[1:3] return?
questions.explanation: Slicing is inclusive of the start index and exclusive of the stop index, so nums[1:3] takes elements at index 1 and 2, giving [20, 30].

questions.question: Which of these reads a file and guarantees it is closed afterwards, even if an error occurs?
questions.explanation: The with statement uses open() as a context manager, which closes the file automatically when the block exits, including on an exception. A bare open() leaves the file open until you call close() yourself.
